name: Atchan
catalog_citation: Russell, Katherine R. 2026. Nasality in Atchan: Synchrony, diachrony and typology. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. 321 pp. eScholarship, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5xq9m6nm (open access).
catalog_locator: Ch. 3 'The phonology of Atchan', §3.4 Tone, printed p. 65 (PDF p. 83); §3.4.1.1 Nouns, printed p. 66 (PDF p. 84); §3.5 Discussion, printed p. 86 (PDF p. 104). …
catalog_quote: Atchan makes use of two contrastive tones – Low (L) and High (H). Four distinct tone levels – High, Mid, Low, and SuperLow – and five contours – High-Low, High-Mid, Mid-Low, Low-SuperLow, and SuperLow-even lower – appear on the surface, all of which are attributable to the interaction of the two underlying tones and a number of regular tonal processes like High-tone spreading and plateauing (Lojenga, 1985; Bôle-Richard, 2008; Russell, 2023). [...] Per the near-identical distribution of tones across these different syllable shapes, I take the tone-bearing unit in Atchan to be the syllable, rather than a smaller unit like the mora. [...] Tone in Atchan bears a high functional load, serving to distinguish both lexical items and grammatical categories. The tone-bearing unit in Atchan is the syllable.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Atchan/Ebrié is a two-tone language (underlying /L/ and /H/; syllable = TBU; lexical melodies /L/, /H/, /LH/, /HL/ on monosyllabic noun roots, plus grammatical tone overlays and polar tones on verbs). The 50-page phonology chapter, and every other opened source, says nothing at all about word stress or accent; no stress position can be assigned. Most roots are monosyllabic CV (66% of 461 roots), verbs 92% monosyllabic.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal notes: some speakers merge /L/ and /LH/ noun classes; voiced obstruents are depressor consonants lowering L in nouns and all tones in verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Description is of lexical and postlexical tone on roots and words in isolation and in phrases (High-tone spreading, plateauing, phrase-position restrictions on surface tone); no word-level stress domain is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Atchan = Ebrié/Cámánncân/Tchaman (ebri1238, ISO ebr), data mainly from the Anono and Blockhauss (Ánonkwathé) villages inside Abidjan collected 2019-2025 with 15+ speakers; Russell's 'Atchan' is the same language as Glottolog's Ebrié. Mobio 2016 concerns the Bidjan-Nkyan variety (no separate glottocode).

sources.note: Ch. 3 'The phonology of Atchan' (pp. 36-87: consonants, vowels, syllable and word structure, tone) describes a two-tone (L/H) system with the syllable as TBU and never mentions stress or accent for Atchan; 'stress' occurs only for Paraguayan Guarani and in bibliography titles, 'accent' only for tone diacritics. §2.3 (pp. 23-25) surveys all earlier descriptions (Delafosse 1904, Vogler 1968, Dumestre 1970/1971, Bole-Richard 1982/2008/2017/2018, Stewart 1966/1973, Kutsch Lojenga 1985, Takouo 2006, Ahoua 2009, Dido 2010/2013/2018, Russell 2023, Jarvis 2025).
